Anomalies (represented as red triangles) are surrounded by ring-shaped normal samples, which cannot be isolated by either x-axis or y-axis slicing cuts. Although these anomalies might be finally isolated by multiple cuts, it results in indistinguishable isolation depth in iTrees compared to normal data. The failure of recalling these anomalies induces high false negative errors. Given that anomalies often contain critical information related to potential accidents or faults, those false negatives may cause serious consequences. Therefore, this issue has been a major bottleneck hindering the performance of iForest, particularly on datasets with high-dimensional/non-linearseparable data spaces.

There have been a number of extensions of iForest introduced over the years [4], [5], [6], [7], [8], [9]. These extensions attempt to devise more advanced isolation methods by (i) using novel hierarchical criteria to selectively pick splitting thresholds and/or dimensions [6], [8], [9] or (ii) using optimal/random hyper-planes [4], [5], [7]. These improvements successfully contribute to better detection performance, but their isolation methods are still confined by linear partition. Instead, data partition in the isolation process is expected to form non-linearly arbitrary shapes in the data space to handle hard anomalies in complicated datasets and eliminate the algorithmic bias in derived anomaly scores. We show two state-of-the-art extensions (PID [6] and EIF [4]) in Fig. 2. PID [6] selectively chooses splitting dimensions

Further, in our specific implementation of DIF, we propose the Computation-Efficient Representation Ensemble method (CERE) and the Deviation-Enhanced Anomaly Scoring function (DEAS). With the help of CERE, DIF can efficiently produce the representation ensemble by taking full advantage of parallel accelerators in the mini-batch calculation, largely eliminating the computational overhead. DEAS leverages the hidden quantitative information enclosed in the mapped dense representations along with qualitative comparisons. This additional information enables a more accurate assessment of the isolation difficulty of data objects, leading to a better anomaly scoring function.

Extensive experiments on a large collection of real-world datasets, including not only tabular data but graph and time series data, show that: (i) DIF significantly outperforms iForest and its state-of-the-art extensions (Sec. 6.2); (ii) DIF also achieves remarkable improvement compared to the ensemble of advanced deep anomaly detectors (Sec. 6.2); (iii) DIF has desired scalability on high-dimensional, largescale datasets (Sec. 6.3) and presents good robustness to anomaly contamination (Sec. 6.4); (iv) the significance of the synergy between random representations and random partition-based isolation is justified by comparing to several alternatives (Sec. 6.5); and (v) the contribution of CERE and DEAS is separately verified in our ablation study (Sec. 6.6).

The mainstream of these extensions focuses on devising more effective isolation methods. SCIF [5] introduces a non-axis-parallel way as branching criteria, i.e., instead of selecting one feature during splitting, an optimal slicing hyper-plane is used. EIF [4] also uses hyper-planes but with random slopes and intercepts. Another work [7] further fixes the empty branching problem of EIF by choosing splitting thresholds from the range of projected values onto the slope direction. PID [6] selectively picks dimensions that have greater variance and selects split points according to the sparsity of the partition branches. The literature [9] proposes a probability-based method to find better split values than random splitting. These extensions normally achieve better performance by introducing non-axis-parallel and/or heuristic partition. However, the major problem is that they still rely on linear isolation operations, which means it is also hard to handle complicated data that require nonlinear partitions as the isolation method. Also, they suffer from the aforementioned artefact problem due to the implicit algorithmic bias hidden in the isolation process. There are also some extensions employing the nearest neighbour information into isolation process, e.g., LeSiNN [22] and iNNE [23]. The literature [24] further uses locally-sensitive hashing to extend the isolation mechanism to any distance measures and data types. These distance-based methods introduce an extra assumption, i.e., anomalies are far from other data objects. However, this assumption does not always hold since clustered anomalies are also very close to their adjacent neighbours [5]. The detection performance is also sensitive to the choice of distance metrics.

Different from many existing studies that only focus on an individual data type, we do not restrict the type of data objects in this work, which means they can be multi-dimensional vectors, time series data, or graphs. For the sake of clarity, we recall the basic procedure of isolation forest (iForest) [3]. A basic structure named isolation tree (iTree for short) is proposed. iTree τ is essentially a binary tree, and each node in the tree corresponds to a pool of data objects. A subset containing n data objects is used as the data pool of the root node, which is randomly subsampled from the whole dataset. iTree τ grows by recursively isolating data objects in the leaf node (i.e., a disjoint partition of data objects into two child nodes) in a topdown fashion until remaining one data object in the node or reaching the maximum depth limit. iForest uses a simple isolation method that performs a comparison between the j-th dimension of the data object o(j) and a splitting value η as the branching criterion of each data object o, where j and η respectively denote a randomly selected feature index and a split value within the range of available values of the j-th feature. Each data object o has a traversing path p(o|τ) in the iTree τ, and length of the traversed path, |p(o|τ)|, can be naturally viewed as an indication of the abnormal degree of o (anomalies are often easier to be isolated with shorter path length). iForest constructs a forest of T iTrees T ={τi}T

These current isolation methods are limited to effectively handle hard anomalies that cannot be isolated using linear partitions on individual features or simple combinations of multiple features. Additionally, these existing methods generally suffer from the algorithmic bias brought by constraints hidden in their isolation strategies.

Let o ∈RD be a vectorised data object. Recall that the branching criterion in DIF is ϕ(o)(j) ≤η. Both iForest and EIF are special cases of DIF when the neural network ϕ is with one linear layer parameterised by a weight matrix W, i.e., ϕ(o) = W⊤o. iForest splits the node by using the criterion o(j) ≤η, while DIF degrades to iForest if the weight matrix is set as an identity matrix, i.e., W = ID. EIF uses a slicing hyper-plane for each node branching, and the slope of its hyper-plane is a normal vector k ∈RD, and k(i) ∼N(0, 1), ∀i ∈{1, · · · D}. The intercept of the hyper-plane p ∈RD is uniformly selected over the range of possible values at each branching point. The branching criterion is (o−p)·k ≤0, which is equivalent to o·k ≤p·k. We can fulfil exactly the same operation in DIF when the weight matrix satisfies W ∈RD×1. The elements in W should also be initialised by a normal distribution N(0, 1) to satisfy W = k. Additionally, the splitting point η = p · k can be understood as a standard random vector p sampled in possible values with a Gaussian noise k.

5.5.3 Synergy between Random Representations and Random Partition-based Isolation DIF employs a novel representation scheme, i.e., the random representation ensemble produced via optimisationfree neural networks. The parameters of these networks can be initialised by randomly sampling from widely-used initialisation distributions (e.g., normal or uniform distribution), easily yielding a set of feature representations with excellent randomness and diversity. Given a sufficiently large set of such random representations, we can largely boost the isolation power in the random data partition, making it possible to effectively isolate some really hard anomalies on some subsets of these representations. This section is organised as follows: In Sec. 6.1, we first start with the experimental setup including the used datasets, competing methods, parameter settings, and evaluation metrics; Sec. 6.2, 6.3, and 6.4 evaluate the performance of our method w.r.t. effectiveness, scalability, and robustness; and in Sec. 6.5 and 6.6, we empirically analyse our method by investigating the significance of the synergy between random representations and random partition-based isolation and the contribution of CERE and DEAS.

Tabular Data. Analysis, Backdoor, DoS, and Exploits are taken from a popular intrusion detection benchmark UNSW NB 15. Following [15], [34], we select different attacks as anomalies in these datasets against normal network traffic. R8 is a highly-imbalanced text classification dataset, where the rare class are treated as anomalies by following [10], [35]. Cover is from the ecology domain. Fraud is for fraudulent credit card transaction detection. Pageblocks and Shuttle are provided by an anomaly benchmark study [36]. 6.1.3 Parameter Settings and Implementations DIF uses 50 representations (r=50) and 6 isolation trees per representation (t=6), with 256 as subsampling size (n=256) for each iTree. DIF processes tabular data by using fullyconnected multi-layer-perceptron networks. All of the IF- based competing methods use 300 trees (the ensemble size is the same as DIF). The subsampling size is set as 256. We use the maximum extension level of EIF, i.e., the extension level is adaptively set as the dimensionality minus 1. For LeSiNN, the subsampling size is 8 by following [22]. As IF- based competitors cannot directly process non-tabular data, we employ the latest powerful unsupervised representation learning models to yield high-quality vectorised representations, and specifically, InfoGraph [41] and TS2Vec [42] are respectively utilised for graph data and time series. Note that InfoGraph uses GIN as its graph encoder architecture, and TS2Vec applies a dilated CNN module with residual blocks. They propose specific learning objectives to optimise generated representations. For the sake of fairness, DIF also respectively utilises the same GIN and CNN network structure to handle graph data and time series but without any optimisation steps. The deep anomaly detectors are trained by 50 epochs and 30 steps per epoch. REPEN, DSVDD, and RECON take an Adam optimiser with a 1e-3 learning rate and use 64 objects per mini-batch, and we empirically found that RDP can work significantly better when using 1e-4. The default/recommended settings are used for the other parameters of these competing methods.

6.1.4 Evaluation Metrics and Computing Infrastructure Following the mainstream evaluation protocols of anomaly detection [3], [4], [15], the detection accuracy is evaluated by two complementary metrics including Area Under the ROC Curve (AUC-ROC) and Area Under the PR Curve (AUC-PR). ROC curve indicates the true positives against false positives, while PR curve summarises precision and recall of the anomaly class only. The paired Wilcoxon signed rank test is used to examine the statistical significance of the performance of DIF against each competing method.
PID and EIF runs out of memory (OOM) on the ultrahigh-dimensional dataset Thrombin. The best performer is boldfaced.

6.2.1 Tabular Data Table 3 and 4 present the AUC-ROC and AUC-PR results of our method DIF and eight competing methods. Overall, DIF largely reduces the false negatives compared to iForest and its three extensions, resulting in substantial averaged performance improvement in detection precision and/or recall rates, and thus, DIF obtains superior AUC-PR and AUC-ROC performance. Particularly, in the average AUC- PR, DIF significantly outperforms EIF (61%), PID (186%), LeSiNN (56%), iForest (144%), eRDP (13%), eREPEN (77%), eDSVDD (19%), and eRECON (82%). DIF also obtains 4% - 11% AUC-ROC improvement across these methods. As shown in Table 3, DIF significantly outperforms isolation-based methods at the 99% confidence level. DIF is the best isolation-based detector across all the ten datasets except AUC-PR on Fraud, on which the nearest neighbourbased anomaly measure LeSiNN is more effective. The

features in Fraud are the results of PCA transformation due to the confidentiality issues, and thus the distance concept used in the nearest neighbour information can well reflect the proximity relationship. By contrast, DIF does not rely on such prior information that is not always reliable in all the datasets. These results demonstrate superior isolation power of DIF, which can effectively isolate anomalies that may not be possible in existing IF-based methods due to the challenges like data sparsity and non-linearity. This is particularly true on challenging high-dimensional datasets like R8, Analysis, Backdoor and DoS.

IF-based anomaly detectors only need CPU devices, while deep ensemble-based methods can leverage GPU acceleration. Therefore, we report the training time of DIF and its deep competitors on both GPU and CPU devices.

Fig. 5 (top) shows the scalability test results of DIF and its competing methods on a CPU device, and Fig. 5 (bottom) reports the comparison using GPU. DIF and all the other isolation-based methods present good scalability w.r.t. both dimensionality and data size compared to deep ensemblebased methods when using CPU computation. This is owed to the subsampling-based methods applied to both data samples and dimensions in isolation-based detectors. Besides, deep ensemble-based methods can greatly benefit from GPU acceleration when handling high-dimensional data. DIF shows outstanding time efficiency compared to its deep ensemble-based counterparts since it only requires one feed-forward step instead of a large number of training epochs. These results demonstrate that DIF inherits excellent computational efficiency from the iForest. Note that DIF can obtain almost the same scalability as iForest w.r.t. the data dimensionality, as DIF performs isolation on newly projected spaces of much smaller dimensionality while iForest works on the original data space.

This section further justifies this intuition by investigating the effectiveness of combining random representations with other anomaly scoring methods, including probability-based anomaly scoring method ECOD [45], distance-based method KNN [46], and densitybased method LOF [47]. **Resolving raw depth definition**

**Documenting CERE assumptions**

**Reviewing remaining paper sections**

The paper specifies 50 representations, six trees per representation, and 256 samples per tree. I also found scoring differences: Equation (8) combines statistics across the whole forest, while the code averages scores computed per representation. I’ll follow the paper’s formula and record that difference, along with the code’s path-length correction and deviation denominator. The contract will also document the code’s representation standardization and keep label-based score adjustment in the fixed evaluator.

content.name: mcp__tsad__record_note
content.arguments: {"contract_id":"score.function","kind":"deviation","text":"Paper Sec. 5.2.2 Eq. (8) and Algorithm 2 integrate both path length and deviation over the full forest T (T=r*t). Official algorithms/dif.py:L245-L275 averages per-representation scores; _cal_score at L454-L463 first computes a depth exponential times mean deviation within each six-tree representation forest. These expressions are generally unequal. Follow the paper: aggregate path lengths and deviations over all r*t trees, then multiply the two terms."}

content.name: mcp__tsad__record_note
content.arguments: {"contract_id":"score.deviation_mean","kind":"deviation","text":"Paper Sec. 5.2.2 Eq. (7) and Algorithm 2 define the arithmetic mean of absolute split deviations over the traversed split nodes, including exact-zero deviations in the node count. Official algorithms/dif.py:L420-L421 instead counts only nonzero deviations and adds 1e-6. Follow the paper: divide by the number of visited internal split nodes; define deviation as zero for a tree with no split nodes."}

content.name: mcp__tsad__record_note
content.arguments: {"contract_id":"score.path_length","kind":"deviation","text":"Paper Sec. 5.2.2 Eq. (8), Sec. 5.3 and Algorithm 2 use the recorded traversed path length |p| and do not specify a terminal-leaf correction. Official algorithms/dif.py:L396-L399 adds c(n_samples_leaf) to the number of traversed edges. Follow the literal paper definition: use traversed edge count without adding the leaf-population correction. Retain standard iForest c(sample_size) as the score normalizer, whose numerical implementation is supplied by official code."}

content.name: mcp__tsad__record_note
content.arguments: {"contract_id":"threshold.protocol","kind":"deviation","text":"Paper Sec. 6.1.4 reports threshold-free AUC-ROC and AUC-PR without specifying label-based segment adjustment. Official utils.py:L199-L220 and L268-L281 replace scores within labeled anomalous segments by the segment maximum and return adjusted metrics, also computing best-test-label F1 in L135-L149. The reproduction returns raw DEAS scores and delegates all thresholding, adjustment and metrics to the fixed EasyTSAD/LiveLeaderBoard evaluator; it never reads test labels."}

content.name: mcp__tsad__record_note
content.arguments: {"contract_id":"model.ensemble_method","kind":"assumption","text":"Use independent CNNs for the time-series backbone, following main_ts.py:L39-L48 (new_ensemble_method=0) and algorithms/dif.py:L214-L229. Paper Sec. 5.2.1 derives CERE using layer weight matrices and Sec. 5.4.1 analyzes its MLP implementation, but gives no concrete CERE convolutional implementation for time series; Sec. 6.1.3 only specifies the TS2Vec-like dilated residual CNN. Do not transfer the tabular MLP CERE setting to the CNN."}

content.name: mcp__tsad__record_note
content.arguments: {"contract_id":"data.representation_preprocess","kind":"issue","text":"Official algorithms/dif.py:L280-L303 fits StandardScaler separately on the entire representation collection in each deep_transfer call, then applies tanh. Because _inference_transfer at L232-L243 calls deep_transfer again for time series, test representations are standardized using their own collection statistics, independently of training statistics. Preserve this algorithm-internal, label-free behavior because the paper is silent; do not silently replace it with train-fitted scaling. Raw-input preprocessing remains raw."}

Nevertheless, its linear axis-parallel isolation method often leads to (i) failure in detecting hard anomalies that are difficult to isolate in high-dimensional/non-linear-separable data space, and (ii) notorious algorithmic bias that assigns unexpectedly lower anomaly scores to artefact regions. These issues contribute to high false negative errors. Several iForest extensions are introduced, but they essentially still employ shallow, linear data partition, restricting their power in isolating true anomalies. Therefore, this paper proposes deep isolation forest. We introduce a new representation scheme that utilises casually initialised neural networks to map original data into random representation ensembles, where random axis-parallel cuts are subsequently applied to perform the data partition. This representation scheme facilitates high freedom of the partition in the original data space (equivalent to non-linear partition on subspaces of varying sizes), encouraging a unique synergy between random representations and random partition-based isolation. Extensive experiments show that our model achieves significant improvement over state-of-the-art isolation-based methods and deep detectors on tabular, graph and time series datasets; our model also inherits desired scalability from iForest.","code_urls":[],"source":"arxiv"},"code_url":"https://github.com/xuhongzuo/deep-iForest","contract":"valid","smoke":{"dataset":"NAB","curves":["Twitter_volume_AAPL","Twitter_volume_AMZN"],"schema":"naive","max_epochs":2,"runs_left":8},"last_smoke":{"n":null,"status":null,"failure_class":null},"notes":{"deviation":4,"assumption":3,"issue":1},"open_questions":[]}

tools.name: bash
tools.description: Execute a bash command (`bash -c`) and return its stdout/stderr. Each call runs in a fresh shell; pass `workdir` instead of using `cd`. Managed `$DSH_*` variables expose current harness environment facts. Long output is truncated to its tail; the full output is saved to a file whose path is reported when available. Provide `description` before `command` in the arguments. Before any delete or move, verify that the resolved absolute target path is the intended one; never run it against a computed path you have not checked. An unset variable expands to an empty string, so guard variables in such paths with `${VAR:?}`. Commands may run under a file sandbox; a blocked file operation is reported as `[sandbox: file access denied under <mode> mode]`, a policy denial: do not retry another way.

description.description: Clear, concise description of what this command does in active voice, 5-10 words (shown in the UI). Examples: "ls" → "List files in current directory"; "git status" → "Show working tree status"; "npm install" → "Install package dependencies".

timeoutMs.description: Timeout in milliseconds. The executor applies its configured default and cap; on expiry the command moves to the background as a job instead of being killed.

workdir.description: Working directory for this command. Defaults to the session workspace; a relative path is resolved against it.

run_in_background.description: Run in the background and return a job id immediately (collect with job_output, stop with job_kill). No timeout applies.

sandbox_permissions.description: The narrowest wider sandbox mode for a one-shot retry of the exact command the sandbox just denied; the retry asks the user for approval.

justification.description: Required with sandbox_permissions: one sentence for the user explaining why this exact command needs the wider access. Use the language of the user’s current request.

include.description: One glob filter for which files to search (e.g. "*.ts", "*.{js,jsx}"). Not a list; negation is not supported.

These issues contribute to high false negative errors. Several iForest extensions are introduced, but they essentially still employ shallow, linear data partition, restricting their power in isolating true anomalies. Therefore, this paper proposes deep isolation forest. We introduce a new representation scheme that utilises casually initialised neural networks to map original data into random representation ensembles, where random axis-parallel cuts are subsequently applied to perform the data partition. 255:                 scores = score_func(x_reduced_lst[i], self.clf_lst[i])
256:                 self.score_lst[i] = scores
257:         else:
258:             # multiprocessing predict
259:             start = np.arange(0, self.n_ensemble, np.ceil(self.n_ensemble / n_processes))
260:             for j in range(int(np.ceil(self.n_ensemble / n_processes))):
261:                 run_id = start + j
262:                 run_id = np.array(np.delete(run_id, np.where(run_id >= self.n_ensemble)), dtype=int)
263:                 if self.verbose >= 1:

268:                                for i in run_id]
269:                 pool.close()
270:                 pool.join()
271: 
272:                 for rid, process in zip(run_id, process_lst):
273:                     self.score_lst[rid] = process.get()

# Original author: Xu Hongzuo (hongzuo.xu@gmail.com), 2022/8/19.
# Apache-2.0; see ../LICENSE and ../NOTICE.
# Modified: TS-only lazy windows; sparse split-path accumulation; paper Eqs.
# (7)-(8) over the complete forest, without leaf correction or zero exclusion.

import random

import numpy as np
import torch
from sklearn.ensemble import IsolationForest
from sklearn.preprocessing import StandardScaler
from torch.utils.data import DataLoader, Dataset

from .net_torch import DilatedConvEncoder


class WindowDataset(Dataset):
    """The official contiguous windows, stored as slices instead of copies."""

    def __init__(self, series, window_size, stride):
        series = np.asarray(series)
        if series.ndim == 1:
            series = series[:, None]
        if series.ndim != 2 or series.shape[1] == 0:
            raise ValueError("Expected a time series with shape [time, channels].")
        if window_size < 1 or stride < 1:
            raise ValueError("Window size and stride must be positive.")
        if len(series) < window_size:
            raise ValueError(
                f"DIFR requires at least {window_size} observations; got {len(series)}."
            )
        if not np.isfinite(series).all():
            raise ValueError("DIFR requires finite input observations.")
        self.series = np.ascontiguousarray(series, dtype=np.float32)
        self.window_size = window_size
        self.stride = stride

    def __len__(self):
        return (len(self.series) - self.window_size) // self.stride + 1

    def __getitem__(self, index):
        start = index * self.stride
        return self.series[start:start + self.window_size]


def average_path_length(n):
    """Official iForest normalizer (not a correction to the observed path)."""
    if n <= 1:
        return 0.0
    if n == 2:
        return 1.0
    return 2.0 * (np.log(n - 1.0) + np.euler_gamma) - 2.0 * (n - 1.0) / n


def tree_statistics(representations, estimator):
    """Return raw edge depth and Eq. (7) for each sample, including zero gaps.

    Sparse decision paths avoid the official sample-by-all-nodes dense matrix.
    Internal node visits equal the number of root-to-leaf edges. Leaf nodes
    have no split feature and are removed before gathering feature values.
    """
    path = estimator.decision_path(representations)
    rows = np.repeat(np.arange(len(representations)), np.diff(path.indptr))
    nodes = path.indices
    tree = estimator.tree_
    is_split = tree.children_left[nodes] != -1
    rows, nodes = rows[is_split], nodes[is_split]
    depth = np.bincount(rows, minlength=len(representations)).astype(np.float64)
    gaps = np.abs(
        representations[rows, tree.feature[nodes]] - tree.threshold[nodes]
    )
    gap_sum = np.bincount(rows, weights=gaps, minlength=len(representations))
    deviation = np.divide(gap_sum, depth, out=np.zeros_like(depth), where=depth > 0)
    return depth, deviation


class DeepIsolationForest:
    """Optimization-free time-series DIF with the approved paper DEAS score.

    All model settings are supplied by the adapter's config dictionary.
    ``representation_preprocess`` and ``score_function`` carry the contract's
    descriptive definitions for the two fixed, non-selectable method stages.
    """

    def __init__(self, params):
        self.params = dict(params)
        p = self.params
        if (p["network_name"] != "dilated_conv" or p["data_type"] != "ts"
                or p["ensemble_method"] != "independent"):
            raise ValueError("DIFR requires independent time-series dilated CNNs.")

            raise ValueError("DIFR uses normally initialized network weights.")
        if p["n_processes"] != 1:
            raise ValueError("The contracted DIFR implementation uses one scoring process.")
        for key in ("window_size", "train_stride", "test_stride", "n_ensemble",
                    "n_estimators", "max_samples", "hidden_dim", "rep_dim",
                    "kernel_size", "dilation_base", "batch_size"):

                raise ValueError(f"{key} must be a positive integer.")

            raise ValueError("layers must be a nonnegative integer.")
        if p["test_stride"] != 1:
            raise ValueError("DIFR's timestamp-aligned test stride must be 1.")
        self.representation_preprocess = p["representation_preprocess"]
        self.score_function = p["score_function"]

        if requested_device.startswith("cuda when available"):
            requested_device = "cuda" if torch.cuda.is_available() else "cpu"
        self.device = torch.device(requested_device)
        self.net_lst = []
        self.clf_lst = []
        self.n_features = None
        self.normalizer_ = None

            torch.cuda.manual_seed_all(seed)
        np.random.seed(seed)
        random.seed(seed)

            dilation_base=p["dilation_base"], activation=p["activation"],
            pooling=p["pooling"], dropout=p["dropout"],
        )

    def deep_transfer(self, windows, net):
        loader = DataLoader(
            windows, batch_size=self.params["batch_size"], drop_last=False,
            shuffle=False, pin_memory=(self.device.type == "cuda"),
        )
        reduced = []
        with torch.no_grad():
            for batch in loader:
                reduced.append(net(batch.to(self.device, dtype=torch.float32)).cpu())
        reduced = torch.cat(reduced).numpy()
        # Official behavior: this scaler is fitted anew for EACH collection,
        # including the full test collection; it is never retained from fit.
        reduced = StandardScaler().fit_transform(reduced)
        return np.ascontiguousarray(np.tanh(reduced), dtype=np.float32)

    def fit(self, series):
        p = self.params
        windows = WindowDataset(series, p["window_size"], p["train_stride"])
        self.n_features = windows.series.shape[1]
        self.net_lst, self.clf_lst = [], []
        self.set_seed(p["random_state"])
        self.ensemble_seeds_ = np.random.randint(0, 100000, p["n_ensemble"])
        sample_size = min(p["max_samples"], len(windows))
        self.normalizer_ = average_path_length(sample_size)
        for seed in self.ensemble_seeds_:
            self.set_seed(seed)
            net = self.make_network(self.n_features).to(self.device)
            for name, param in net.named_parameters():

            forest = IsolationForest(
                n_estimators=p["n_estimators"], max_samples=sample_size,
                random_state=int(seed),
            )
            forest.fit(reduced)
            self.net_lst.append(net)
            self.clf_lst.append(forest)
        return self

    def decision_function(self, series):
        if not self.clf_lst:
            raise RuntimeError("Fit DIFR before computing anomaly scores.")
        p = self.params
        windows = WindowDataset(series, p["window_size"], p["test_stride"])
        if windows.series.shape[1] != self.n_features:
            raise ValueError("Train and test channel counts must match.")
        depth_sum = np.zeros(len(windows), dtype=np.float64)
        deviation_sum = np.zeros_like(depth_sum)
        if self.normalizer_ == 0:
            return deviation_sum

            reduced = self.deep_transfer(windows, net)
            for estimator in forest.estimators_:
                depth, deviation = tree_statistics(reduced, estimator)
                depth_sum += depth
                deviation_sum += deviation
                tree_count += 1
        # Eq. (8) is a product of global means over ALL representation trees.
        # It is not the mean of separate per-representation products.
        return np.exp2(-depth_sum / (tree_count * self.normalizer_)) * (
            deviation_sum / tree_count
        )

    deviation = np.divide(gap_sum, depth, out=np.zeros_like(depth), where=depth > 0)
    return depth, deviation


class DeepIsolationForest:
    """Optimization-free time-series DIF with the approved paper DEAS score.

    All model settings are supplied by the adapter's config dictionary.
    ``representation_preprocess`` and ``score_function`` carry the contract's
    descriptive definitions for the two fixed, non-selectable method stages.
    """

    def __init__(self, params):
        self.params = dict(params)
        p = self.params
        if (p["network_name"] != "dilated_conv" or p["data_type"] != "ts"
                or p["ensemble_method"] != "independent"):
            raise ValueError("DIFR requires independent time-series dilated CNNs.")
        if p["init_distribution"] != "normal":
            raise ValueError("DIFR uses normally initialized network weights.")
        if p["n_processes"] != 1:
            raise ValueError("The contracted DIFR implementation uses one scoring process.")
        for key in ("window_size", "train_stride", "test_stride", "n_ensemble",
                    "n_estimators", "max_samples", "hidden_dim", "rep_dim",
                    "kernel_size", "dilation_base", "batch_size"):
            if not isinstance(p[key], int) or p[key] < 1:
                raise ValueError(f"{key} must be a positive integer.")
        if not isinstance(p["layers"], int) or p["layers"] < 0:
            raise ValueError("layers must be a nonnegative integer.")
        if p["test_stride"] != 1:
            raise ValueError("DIFR's timestamp-aligned test stride must be 1.")
        self.representation_preprocess = p["representation_preprocess"]
        self.score_function = p["score_function"]
        requested_device = p["device"]
        if requested_device.startswith("cuda when available"):
            requested_device = "cuda" if torch.cuda.is_available() else "cpu"
        self.device = torch.device(requested_device)
        self.net_lst = []
        self.clf_lst = []
        self.n_features = None
        self.normalizer_ = None

    @staticmethod
    def set_seed(seed):
        seed = int(seed)
        torch.manual_seed(seed)
        if torch.cuda.is_available():
            torch.cuda.manual_seed(seed)
            torch.cuda.manual_seed_all(seed)
        np.random.seed(seed)
        random.seed(seed)

    def make_network(self, n_features):
        p = self.params
        return DilatedConvEncoder(
            n_features, hidden_dim=p["hidden_dim"], rep_dim=p["rep_dim"],
            layers=p["layers"], kernel_size=p["kernel_size"],
            dilation_base=p["dilation_base"], activation=p["activation"],
            pooling=p["pooling"], dropout=p["dropout"],
        )

    def deep_transfer(self, windows, net):
        loader = DataLoader(
            windows, batch_size=self.params["batch_size"], drop_last=False,
            shuffle=False, pin_memory=(self.device.type == "cuda"),
        )
        reduced = []
        with torch.no_grad():
            for batch in loader:
                reduced.append(net(batch.to(self.device, dtype=torch.float32)).cpu())
        reduced = torch.cat(reduced).numpy()
        # Official behavior: this scaler is fitted anew for EACH collection,
        # including the full test collection; it is never retained from fit.
        reduced = StandardScaler().fit_transform(reduced)
        return np.ascontiguousarray(np.tanh(reduced), dtype=np.float32)

    def fit(self, series):
        p = self.params
        windows = WindowDataset(series, p["window_size"], p["train_stride"])
        self.n_features = windows.series.shape[1]
        self.net_lst, self.clf_lst = [], []
        self.set_seed(p["random_state"])
        self.ensemble_seeds_ = np.random.randint(0, 100000, p["n_ensemble"])
        sample_size = min(p["max_samples"], len(windows))
        self.normalizer_ = average_path_length(sample_size)
        for seed in self.ensemble_seeds_:
            self.set_seed(seed)
            net = self.make_network(self.n_features).to(self.device)
            for name, param in net.named_parameters():
                if name.endswith("weight"):
                    torch.nn.init.normal_(param, mean=p["init_mean"], std=p["init_std"])
            net.requires_grad_(False)
            net.eval()
            reduced = self.deep_transfer(windows, net)
            forest = IsolationForest(
                n_estimators=p["n_estimators"], max_samples=sample_size,
                random_state=int(seed),
            )
            forest.fit(reduced)
            self.net_lst.append(net)
            self.clf_lst.append(forest)
        return self

    def decision_function(self, series):
        if not self.clf_lst:
            raise RuntimeError("Fit DIFR before computing anomaly scores.")
        p = self.params
        windows = WindowDataset(series, p["window_size"], p["test_stride"])
        if windows.series.shape[1] != self.n_features:
            raise ValueError("Train and test channel counts must match.")
        depth_sum = np.zeros(len(windows), dtype=np.float64)
        deviation_sum = np.zeros_like(depth_sum)
        if self.normalizer_ == 0:
            return deviation_sum
        tree_count = 0
        for net, forest in zip(self.net_lst, self.clf_lst):
            reduced = self.deep_transfer(windows, net)
            for estimator in forest.estimators_:
                depth, deviation = tree_statistics(reduced, estimator)
                depth_sum += depth
                deviation_sum += deviation
                tree_count += 1
        # Eq. (8) is a product of global means over ALL representation trees.
        # It is not the mean of separate per-representation products.
        return np.exp2(-depth_sum / (tree_count * self.normalizer_)) * (
            deviation_sum / tree_count
        )

49:     if n <= 1:

56: def tree_statistics(representations, estimator):
57:     """Return raw edge depth and Eq. (7) for each sample, including zero gaps.
58: 
59:     Sparse decision paths avoid the official sample-by-all-nodes dense matrix.
60:     Internal node visits equal the number of root-to-leaf edges. Leaf nodes
61:     have no split feature and are removed before gathering feature values.
62:     """
63:     path = estimator.decision_path(representations)
64:     rows = np.repeat(np.arange(len(representations)), np.diff(path.indptr))
65:     nodes = path.indices
66:     tree = estimator.tree_
67:     is_split = tree.children_left[nodes] != -1
68:     rows, nodes = rows[is_split], nodes[is_split]
69:     depth = np.bincount(rows, minlength=len(representations)).astype(np.float64)
70:     gaps = np.abs(
71:         representations[rows, tree.feature[nodes]] - tree.threshold[nodes]
72:     )
73:     gap_sum = np.bincount(rows, weights=gaps, minlength=len(representations))
74:     deviation = np.divide(gap_sum, depth, out=np.zeros_like(depth), where=depth > 0)
75:     return depth, deviation

{"content":""""EasyTSAD adapter for the contract-defined time-series deep isolation forest."""

import numpy as np

from .. import BaseMethod
from ...DataFactory import TSData
from .src import DeepIsolationForest


class DIFR(BaseMethod):
    def __init__(self, params: dict):
        super().__init__()
        self.model = DeepIsolationForest(params)
        self._scores = None

    def train_valid_phase(self, tsTrain: TSData):
        # The official TS experiment fits on train alone, without optimization.
        self._scores = None
        self.model.fit(tsTrain.train)

    def test_phase(self, tsData: TSData):
        self._scores = self.model.decision_function(tsData.test)

    def anomaly_score(self) -> np.ndarray:
        if self._scores is None:
            raise RuntimeError("Call test_phase before requesting DIFR scores.")
        # Full-window scores are a suffix: index i belongs to i+window_size-1.
        return self._scores

    def param_statistic(self, save_file):
        # This hook is called before fitting, so the channel count is unknown.
        # State the assumption explicitly instead of constructing a dummy net.
        with open(save_file, "w", encoding="utf-8") as handle:
            handle.write(
                "DIFR uses fixed random CNNs and isolation trees; no trainable "
                "optimization parameters.\n"
                f"Representation ensemble: {self.model.params['n_ensemble']}\n"
                f"Trees per representation: {self.model.params['n_estimators']}\n"
            )

{"content":""""Short deterministic CPU checks: python -m EasyTSAD.Methods.DIFR.selftest."""

from pathlib import Path
from types import SimpleNamespace
import json
import tomllib

import numpy as np
import torch
from sklearn.tree import DecisionTreeRegressor

from .DIFR import DIFR
from .src import DeepIsolationForest
from .src.dif import WindowDataset, average_path_length, tree_statistics


def reference_scores(model, series):
    """Independent literal root-to-leaf traversal and full-forest Eq. (8)."""
    p = model.params
    windows = WindowDataset(series, p["window_size"], p["test_stride"])
    all_depths, all_deviations = [], []
    for net, forest in zip(model.net_lst, model.clf_lst):
        reps = model.deep_transfer(windows, net)
        for estimator in forest.estimators_:
            tree = estimator.tree_
            depths, deviations = [], []
            for row in reps:
                node, gaps = 0, []
                while tree.children_left[node] != -1:
                    value = row[tree.feature[node]]
                    gaps.append(abs(float(value) - tree.threshold[node]))
                    node = (tree.children_left[node] if value <= tree.threshold[node]
                            else tree.children_right[node])
                depths.append(len(gaps))
                deviations.append(sum(gaps) / len(gaps) if gaps else 0.0)
            all_depths.append(depths)
            all_deviations.append(deviations)
    if model.normalizer_ == 0:
        return np.zeros(len(windows))
    return np.exp2(-np.mean(all_depths, axis=0) / model.normalizer_) * np.mean(
        all_deviations, axis=0
    )


def main():
    # This only limits the tiny CPU self-test, never the detector's runtime.
    torch.set_num_threads(1)
    method = Path(__file__).resolve().parent
    config = tomllib.loads((method / "config.toml").read_text())
    params = config["Model_Params"]["Default"]
    root = method.parents[2]
    contract = json.loads((root / "EasyTSAD/Harness/tasks/DIFR/contract.json").read_text())
    for claim in contract["claims"]:
        key = claim.get("config_key")
        if key:
            actual = (config["Data_Params"][key.split(".", 1)[1]]
                      if key.startswith("Data_Params.") else params[key])
            assert actual == claim["value"], claim["id"]
    registry = tomllib.loads((root / "envs/registry.toml").read_text())
    assert [name for name, env in registry["envs"].items()
            if "DIFR" in env["methods"]] == ["torch2"]
    params = dict(params, device="cpu")
    rng = np.random.RandomState(19)
    train = rng.normal(size=(360, 1)).astype(np.float32)
    test = rng.normal(size=(118, 1)).astype(np.float32)
    windows = WindowDataset(train, params["window_size"], params["train_stride"])
    expected = np.array([train[i:i + params["window_size"]]
                         for i in range(0, len(train) - params["window_size"] + 1,
                                        params["train_stride"])])
    np.testing.assert_array_equal(np.stack([windows[i] for i in range(len(windows))]), expected)

    adapter = DIFR(params)
    # Validation and labels deliberately are not provided: the adapter uses neither.
    adapter.train_valid_phase(SimpleNamespace(train=train[:, 0]))
    adapter.test_phase(SimpleNamespace(test=test[:, 0]))
    scores = adapter.anomaly_score()
    assert scores.shape == (len(test) - params["window_size"] + 1,)
    assert np.isfinite(scores).all() and (scores >= 0).all()
    assert len(adapter.model.net_lst) == params["n_ensemble"]
    assert sum(len(f.estimators_) for f in adapter.model.clf_lst) == (
        params["n_ensemble"] * params["n_estimators"]
    )
    np.testing.assert_allclose(scores, reference_scores(adapter.model, test), rtol=1e-12)
    assert all(not parameter.requires_grad
               for net in adapter.model.net_lst for parameter in net.parameters())
    for seed, net in zip(adapter.model.ensemble_seeds_, adapter.model.net_lst):
        # The official seed/init order must reproduce every parameter exactly.
        adapter.model.set_seed(seed)
        clone = adapter.model.make_network(1)
        for name, param in clone.named_parameters():
            if name.endswith("weight"):
                torch.nn.init.normal_(param, mean=params["init_mean"], std=params["init_std"])
        assert all(torch.equal(a, b) for a, b in zip(net.parameters(), clone.parameters()))
    np.testing.assert_array_equal(adapter.model.decision_function(test), scores)

    # A threshold of exactly zero verifies that zero gaps count in the denominator.
    tree = DecisionTreeRegressor(max_depth=1, random_state=0).fit(
        np.array([[-1.0], [1.0]], dtype=np.float32), [0.0, 1.0]
    )
    depth, deviation = tree_statistics(np.array([[-1.0], [0.0], [1.0]], dtype=np.float32), tree)
    np.testing.assert_array_equal(depth, [1.0, 1.0, 1.0])
    np.testing.assert_array_equal(deviation, [1.0, 0.0, 1.0])
    assert average_path_length(1) == 0 and average_path_length(2) == 1

    mts = DeepIsolationForest(params).fit(rng.normal(size=(360, 3)))
    mts_test = rng.normal(size=(118, 3))
    mts_scores = mts.decision_function(mts_test)
    assert mts_scores.shape == scores.shape and np.isfinite(mts_scores).all()
    np.testing.assert_allclose(mts_scores, reference_scores(mts, mts_test), rtol=1e-12)
    constant = DeepIsolationForest(params).fit(np.zeros(360))
    np.testing.assert_array_equal(constant.decision_function(np.zeros(118)), np.zeros_like(scores))
    one_window = DeepIsolationForest(params).fit(np.zeros(params["window_size"]))
    np.testing.assert_array_equal(one_window.decision_function(test), np.zeros_like(scores))
    try:
        adapter.model.decision_function(np.zeros(params["window_size"] - 1))
    except ValueError as exc:
        assert "at least" in str(exc)
    else:
        raise AssertionError("Short input must raise an informative error")
    print("PASS: 27 config mappings, unique registration, UTS/MTS forward fitting/scoring,")
    print("independent full-forest DEAS reference, exact initialization, repeatability,")
    print("window alignment, zero gaps, constant trees, one-window forest, short-input error.")


if __name__ == "__main__":
    main()

    torch.set_num_threads(1)
    method = Path(__file__).resolve().parent
    config = tomllib.loads((method / "config.toml").read_text())
    params = config["Model_Params"]["Default"]
    root = method.parents[2]
    contract = json.loads((root / "EasyTSAD/Harness/tasks/DIFR/contract.json").read_text())
    for claim in contract["claims"]:
        key = claim.get("config_key")
        if key:
            actual = (config["Data_Params"][key.split(".", 1)[1]]
                      if key.startswith("Data_Params.") else params[key])
            assert actual == claim["value"], claim["id"]
    registry = tomllib.loads((root / "envs/registry.toml").read_text())
    assert [name for name, env in registry["envs"].items()
            if "DIFR" in env["methods"]] == ["torch2"]
    params = dict(params, device="cpu")
    rng = np.random.RandomState(19)
    train = rng.normal(size=(360, 1)).astype(np.float32)
    test = rng.normal(size=(118, 1)).astype(np.float32)
    windows = WindowDataset(train, params["window_size"], params["train_stride"])
    expected = np.array([train[i:i + params["window_size"]]
                         for i in range(0, len(train) - params["window_size"] + 1,
                                        params["train_stride"])])
    np.testing.assert_array_equal(np.stack([windows[i] for i in range(len(windows))]), expected)

    adapter = DIFR(params)
    # Validation and labels deliberately are not provided: the adapter uses neither.
    adapter.train_valid_phase(SimpleNamespace(train=train[:, 0]))
    adapter.test_phase(SimpleNamespace(test=test[:, 0]))
    scores = adapter.anomaly_score()
    assert scores.shape == (len(test) - params["window_size"] + 1,)
    assert np.isfinite(scores).all() and (scores >= 0).all()
    assert len(adapter.model.net_lst) == params["n_ensemble"]
    assert sum(len(f.estimators_) for f in adapter.model.clf_lst) == (
        params["n_ensemble"] * params["n_estimators"]
    )
    np.testing.assert_allclose(scores, reference_scores(adapter.model, test), rtol=1e-12)
    assert all(not parameter.requires_grad
               for net in adapter.model.net_lst for parameter in net.parameters())
    for seed, net in zip(adapter.model.ensemble_seeds_, adapter.model.net_lst):
        # The official seed/init order must reproduce every parameter exactly.
        adapter.model.set_seed(seed)
        clone = adapter.model.make_network(1)
        for name, param in clone.named_parameters():
            if name.endswith("weight"):
                torch.nn.init.normal_(param, mean=params["init_mean"], std=params["init_std"])
        assert all(torch.equal(a, b) for a, b in zip(net.parameters(), clone.parameters()))
    np.testing.assert_array_equal(adapter.model.decision_function(test), scores)

    # A threshold of exactly zero verifies that zero gaps count in the denominator.
    tree = DecisionTreeRegressor(max_depth=1, random_state=0).fit(
        np.array([[-1.0], [1.0]], dtype=np.float32), [0.0, 1.0]
    )
    depth, deviation = tree_statistics(np.array([[-1.0], [0.0], [1.0]], dtype=np.float32), tree)
    np.testing.assert_array_equal(depth, [1.0, 1.0, 1.0])
    np.testing.assert_array_equal(deviation, [1.0, 0.0, 1.0])
    assert average_path_length(1) == 0 and average_path_length(2) == 1

    mts = DeepIsolationForest(params).fit(rng.normal(size=(360, 3)))
    mts_test = rng.normal(size=(118, 3))
    mts_scores = mts.decision_function(mts_test)
    assert mts_scores.shape == scores.shape and np.isfinite(mts_scores).all()
    np.testing.assert_allclose(mts_scores, reference_scores(mts, mts_test), rtol=1e-12)
    constant = DeepIsolationForest(params).fit(np.zeros(360))
    np.testing.assert_array_equal(constant.decision_function(np.zeros(118)), np.zeros_like(scores))
    one_window = DeepIsolationForest(params).fit(np.zeros(params["window_size"]))
    np.testing.assert_array_equal(one_window.decision_function(test), np.zeros_like(scores))
    try:
        adapter.model.decision_function(np.zeros(params["window_size"] - 1))
    except ValueError as exc:
        assert "at least" in str(exc)
    else:
        raise AssertionError("Short input must raise an informative error")
    print("PASS: 27 config mappings, unique registration, UTS/MTS forward fitting/scoring,")
    print("independent full-forest DEAS reference, exact initialization, repeatability,")
    print("window alignment, zero gaps, constant trees, one-window forest, short-input error.")


if __name__ == "__main__":
    main()

{"content":"# DIFR

EasyTSAD adapter for Deep Isolation Forest for Anomaly Detection
(arXiv:2206.06602), using the approved time-series reproduction contract.

`src/net_torch.py` adapts the official TS2Vec-style residual dilated CNN.
`src/dif.py` contains window construction, random representation extraction,
isolation forests, and scoring, with no framework imports. `DIFR.py` passes
training and test values to the algorithm and returns the score suffix.

All 27 contract claims carrying a `config_key` are copied verbatim into
`config.toml`. The long representation preprocessing, score function, and
device strings are intentional: they match the approved contract exactly.
No model defaults are duplicated in the adapter or algorithm constructors.

The method uses 100-point full windows, training stride 10 and test stride 1,
50 fixed random CNNs, and 6 isolation trees per representation with at most
256 training windows per tree. There is no optimization, loss, learning rate,
or training epoch loop. Training uses only the supplied training series.
Both univariate and jointly processed multivariate arrays are supported.

Following the official time-series code, every network's representations are
standardized and passed through tanh. The scaler is fitted separately to each
complete training or test representation collection. Test scaling therefore
uses the unlabeled test collection's statistics and is not an online procedure.

Following the approved paper interpretation, DEAS combines statistics across
all 300 trees: `2**(-mean(path_length)/c(sample_size))*mean(deviation)`.

tools.description: Execute a bash command (`bash -c`) and return its stdout/stderr. Each call runs in a fresh shell; pass `workdir` instead of using `cd`. Managed `$DSH_*` variables expose current harness environment facts. Long output is truncated to its tail; the full output is saved to a file whose path is reported when available. Provide `description` before `command` in the arguments. Before any delete or move, verify that the resolved absolute target path is the intended one; never run it against a computed path you have not checked. An unset variable expands to an empty string, so guard variables in such paths with `${VAR:?}`. Commands may run under a file sandbox; a blocked file operation is reported as `[sandbox: file access denied under <mode> mode]`, a policy denial: do not retry another way.
